name: Spain
traditionNote: A codified civil-law system with an unusual twist in Article 1(6) of the Civil Code: repeated Tribunal Supremo rulings form doctrina jurisprudencial, which complements the legal order and can itself be a ground of appeal, without being precedent in the common-law sense.
summary: A statute (ley) is passed by the Congreso de los Diputados, reviewed by the Senado — whose veto or amendments the Congress can override — sanctioned and promulgated by the King, and published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado. It enters into force twenty days after complete publication in the BOE unless it provides otherwise. The Government legislates directly in two forms the Constitution allows: the real decreto-ley, an emergency instrument that must be validated by the Congress within thirty days, and the real decreto legislativo, a delegated consolidation or code made under a statutory mandate. Below them, reglamentos take the form of real decretos of the Council of Ministers and ministerial orders, published in the same gazette. Since 1 January 2009 the electronic edition of the BOE is the official one and the printed edition has ceased; publication is what makes a norm effective, and the BOE's own consolidated texts carry a notice on every page saying that they are informative and have no legal value. Spain is also profoundly decentralised: seventeen autonomous communities legislate within their statutes of autonomy, publish in their own gazettes, and in six of them do so in a co-official language alongside Spanish.
hierarchy: EU law and treaties validly concluded and published in Spain, which under Article 96 form part of the internal order
Estatutos de autonomía — the statutes of autonomy of the seventeen communities, organic statutes standing between the Constitution and ordinary law
Ley orgánica — organic statutes on fundamental rights, electoral law and the statutes themselves, requiring an absolute majority of the Congress
Ley ordinaria, real decreto-ley and real decreto legislativo — ordinary statutes and the two forms of government legislation
Reglamentos — real decretos of the Council of Ministers, then ministerial orders and lower instruments
Autonomic and local law — the statutes and regulations of the communities within their competences, and municipal ordinances below them

gazette.name: Boletin Oficial del Estado
gazette.authority: Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado, Ministerio de la Presidencia
gazette.coverage: Daily since 1936, with its predecessor the Gaceta de Madrid digitised back to 1661 in a separate collection; the electronic edition has been the official one since 1 January 2009
gazette.desc: The gazette in which a Spanish norm is published and thereby becomes effective. Each item has a permanent identifier of the form BOE-A-1978-31229 and an ELI address, and the daily issue is divided into sections — general provisions, authorities and personnel, other provisions, announcements — that tell you the rank of what you are reading before you read it.
gazette.howto: 'Último BOE' opens today's issue and the calendar reaches any past day; 'Buscar en BOE' searches the diary itself. The identifier resolves directly — boe.es/diario_boe/txt.php?id=BOE-A-1978-31229 — as does the European identifier, boe.es/eli/es/c/1978/12/27/(1). Sections are worth using as a filter: a rule of general application is in Sección I, and something in Sección III is usually not.
gazette.note: The signed electronic edition is authentic; a print-out is not. The BOE also publishes items in the co-official languages by agreement with several communities, but the Spanish text is the one that governs.

constitution.name: Constitucion Espanola
constitution.authority: Approved by referendum 6 December 1978; published in the BOE of 29 December 1978
constitution.coverage: In force since 29 December 1978, amended only twice — Article 13(2) in 1992 and Article 135 in 2011 — with a third amendment in 2024 replacing the word 'disminuidos' in Article 49
constitution.desc: The 1978 settlement: a parliamentary monarchy, a catalogue of fundamental rights enforceable by amparo before the Constitutional Court, and a territorial model that left the map of competences to be filled in by statutes of autonomy rather than fixed in the text.
constitution.howto: The consolidated page shows the current text with its amendment history in the 'análisis' panel; the tabs there also list the norms that develop it. The Congress publishes the official English, French, German and co-official language versions at constitucion.congreso.es.
constitution.note: Ordinary amendment needs three-fifths of both chambers; touching the preliminary title, the fundamental-rights section or the Crown triggers the aggravated procedure — two-thirds, dissolution, re-approval by the new chambers and a referendum.

sources.name: Legislacion consolidada (BOE)
sources.authority: Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado
sources.coverage: State legislation of general application in force, with every version the norm has had since consolidation began, and the amendment history recorded article by article
sources.desc: The version Spanish practice reads, maintained by the gazette itself rather than by a publisher. Its distinctive feature is the 'análisis' panel: for any norm it lists what it modified, what modified it, what it repealed and what repealed it, and the case law of the Constitutional Court affecting it.
sources.howto: Search by title, date, department or identifier, then use the version selector to read the text as it stood on a given date, and 'análisis' for the amendment map. Every article carries the reference to the norm that gave it its current wording.
sources.note: Every consolidated page says it plainly: the text is informative and has no legal value. The published BOE item is the authentic one.

sources.name: Codigos electronicos (BOE)
sources.authority: Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado
sources.coverage: Several hundred compilations by subject, each gathering the consolidated norms of a field into one file, updated as the underlying texts change
sources.desc: Spain's answer to the problem that a field of law is never one statute. Each código is a curated bundle — civil, criminal, labour, tax, administrative procedure, data protection — downloadable whole as PDF or ePub, which makes it the fastest way to acquire a whole area at once.
sources.howto: Browse the catalogue by subject, or take the university codes collection, which is trimmed to teaching use. Each code states its update date; the same texts consolidated individually are in the legislation search.
sources.note: Compilations of consolidated texts, and therefore informative in the same way — useful for reading, not for citing the authentic wording.

sources.name: Gazeta (1661-1959)
sources.authority: Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado
sources.coverage: The Gaceta de Madrid and its successors, digitised from 1661 to 1959, including the parallel gazettes of the Civil War period
sources.desc: Three centuries of Spanish official publication, scanned and searchable. It matters practically as well as historically: nineteenth-century statutes still in force — parts of the Civil Code among them — were published here, and this is where their original text is.
sources.howto: Search by date, keyword or reference; results are page images of the original issue. Norms still in force will usually also have a consolidated page in the modern legislation search, with the Gazeta item as their origin.
sources.note: Scanned images with full-text search over the OCR, so the search misses what the OCR misread.

sources.name: BORME
sources.en: Official Gazette of the Commercial Register
sources.authority: Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado, publishing entries supplied by the Registro Mercantil
sources.coverage: Daily, with entries by province and company; searchable back through the electronic era
sources.desc: The company gazette: incorporations, appointments and removals of directors, capital changes, mergers, insolvency entries. Not a source of law, but the publication that makes company facts opposable to third parties.
sources.howto: Open the day's issue or search by company name or province; entries are short and reference the register file rather than reproducing the deed.
sources.note: The register entry itself, not the BORME notice, is the primary record; the notice publishes it.

sources.name: Otros diarios oficiales
sources.native: Otros diarios oficiales — boletines autonómicos y provinciales
sources.authority: Each autonomous community and province publishes its own; the index is kept by the BOE
sources.coverage: The seventeen autonomic gazettes and the provincial bulletins, with links to each
sources.desc: Where the other half of Spanish law is published. An autonomic statute is promulgated in that community's gazette — DOGC in Catalonia, BOJA in Andalusia, BOPV in the Basque Country — and municipal ordinances appear in the provincial bulletin, not in the BOE.
sources.howto: Pick the community or province from the index and follow into its gazette, each of which has its own search. Autonomic statutes are additionally reproduced in the BOE, so a Catalan or Galician ley can also be found in the state gazette and in the state consolidated legislation.
sources.note: In the communities with a co-official language, both versions are official; where they diverge the community's own rules settle which prevails.

sources.name: CENDOJ — buscador de jurisprudencia
sources.authority: Centro de Documentación Judicial, Consejo General del Poder Judicial
sources.coverage: Decisions of the Tribunal Supremo, the Audiencia Nacional, the superior courts of justice of the communities and the provincial audiencias, anonymised, with ECLI identifiers
sources.desc: The judiciary's own database and the only free route to Spanish case law in bulk. Repeated Supreme Court holdings are what Article 1(6) of the Civil Code calls doctrina jurisprudencial — not binding precedent, but a ground on which a judgment can be appealed for departing from it.
sources.howto: Search by court, date, ECLI or the number of the resolution, or by free text with the field filters; the Tribunal Supremo's decisions can be isolated by choosing the court and its chamber (sala primera for civil, segunda for criminal, tercera for administrative, cuarta for labour).
sources.note: Anonymised, and selective at the lower levels. The full text supplied by the court is the reference; commercial databases add headnotes that are not part of the judgment.

sources.name: Buscador de jurisprudencia constitucional
sources.coverage: Every decision of the Constitutional Court since 1980 — sentencias, autos and providencias — with the pleadings, dissenting opinions and the norms at issue
sources.desc: Spain's constitutional court sits outside the ordinary judiciary and can annul a statute with effect for everyone. Its case law is indexed here against the constitutional articles and the norms challenged, which makes it possible to ask 'what has the Court said about this article' directly.
sources.howto: Search by decision number and year — STC 31/2010 — by the norm challenged, or by constitutional article; the record shows the type of proceeding, which matters, since an amparo binds the parties while a recurso de inconstitucionalidad can strike a statute down for everyone.
sources.note: Decisions declaring a norm unconstitutional are also published in the BOE, and the consolidated text of the affected norm records them in its 'análisis' panel.

sources.name: Congreso de los Diputados
sources.coverage: Bills and their stages, the Diario de Sesiones, the Boletín Oficial de las Cortes Generales, committee work and votes, by legislature
sources.desc: Where a bill is followed and where the record of what was said about it lives. The Boletín Oficial de las Cortes Generales carries the successive texts of a bill with the amendments tabled, which is the material for arguing legislative intent.
sources.howto: Use the legislative initiatives search filtered by type and legislature; each initiative page shows the stages with links to the BOCG texts and the session records. Note that a decreto-ley appears here as a validation debate rather than as a bill, unless the Congress converts it.
sources.note: The Senate's own site holds the second-chamber stage; it answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Dictamenes del Consejo de Estado
sources.native: Buscador de dictámenes del Consejo de Estado
sources.en: Opinions of the Council of State
sources.authority: Consejo de Estado; database hosted by the BOE
sources.coverage: The Council's opinions, searchable by number, year, subject and the norm concerned
sources.desc: The supreme consultative body of the Government. Its opinion is required before most regulations are approved and before certain administrative decisions, so a dictamen is often the fullest analysis in existence of why a rule takes the form it does.
sources.howto: Search by year and number or by subject; opinions cite the draft they examined, which lets you pair a dictamen with the real decreto that eventually appeared in the BOE.
sources.note: An opinion is advisory. Where it was required and not obtained, however, the resulting regulation can be annulled for that reason alone.

sources.name: Doctrina de la Fiscalia
sources.native: Buscador de doctrina de la Fiscalía
sources.authority: Fiscalía General del Estado; database hosted by the BOE
sources.coverage: Circulars, instructions and consultations of the Attorney General, which bind prosecutors internally
sources.desc: How the prosecution service reads the criminal law. These instruments do not bind courts, but they determine what will be charged and how, which in practice settles a great deal of criminal law before any judge sees it.
sources.howto: Search by type — circular, instrucción, consulta — with year and subject; each states the provisions it interprets.
sources.note: Internal doctrine, not law. Courts routinely depart from it.

sources.name: Datos abiertos del BOE
sources.authority: Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado
sources.coverage: The daily issues of the BOE and BORME, consolidated legislation and the auxiliary tables, as XML and through a documented API
sources.desc: Spain publishes its gazette as structured data, addressed by the same identifiers as the website — which makes the whole corpus retrievable rather than scrapeable, and is why so many Spanish legal tools are built on top of it.
sources.howto: Read the API documentation, then request a summary of a day's issue or a specific item by its BOE-A identifier; the ELI scheme addresses norms in the consolidated collection.

sources.name: Constitution in English (Congreso)
sources.native: Constitución Española — versiones en otros idiomas
sources.coverage: The full text of the 1978 Constitution with its amendments, in the co-official languages and in English, French and German
sources.desc: The Congress's own site for the Constitution, article by article, with the parliamentary history of the drafting attached — the closest thing Spain has to an official English constitutional text.
sources.howto: Switch language from the top of the site and read by title and article; the Spanish version links each article to the debates that produced it.
sources.note: A translation, with no legal force. Spanish statutes generally are not translated by the state at all.

sources.name: EUR-Lex (en espanol)
sources.native: EUR-Lex — Derecho de la Unión Europea
sources.authority: Oficina de Publicaciones de la Unión Europea (Publications Office of the European Union)
sources.coverage: EU treaties, legislation, consolidated texts, case law and national implementing measures, in Spanish among the official languages
sources.desc: The BOE carries no EU legislation, and a regulation applies in Spain without any Spanish norm at all. The BOE's own 'Derecho de la Unión Europea' section is a signpost to here.
sources.howto: Search by CELEX number or subject with the interface in Spanish; the national implementing measures tab on a directive lists the Spanish norms notified for it.
sources.note: The Spanish language version of an EU act is authentic alongside the others; the Official Journal edition is the binding one.

sources.name: vLex
sources.coverage: Legislation, case law including unpublished decisions, commentary and practice material for Spain and Latin America
sources.desc: With Aranzadi and La Ley, one of the services Spanish practice runs on. Worth naming because it aggregates the state and autonomic sources with case law from courts whose own publication is thin, and because Spanish citations often point at it rather than at the BOE.
sources.howto: Some content is readable without a subscription and most is not; the free state sources above cover the texts themselves.
sources.note: Private and commercial. Its consolidated texts are editorial work — for the authentic wording, return to the BOE item.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a Spanish statute
findLaw.steps: Search the consolidated legislation by title or identifier and open the norm. Use the version selector to confirm you are reading the text in force today, and the 'análisis' panel to see every modification made to it. Remember the banner: the consolidated text is informative and has no legal value.

findLaw.task: Read the norm exactly as published
findLaw.steps: Take the BOE identifier from the head of the consolidated text — BOE-A-1978-31229 — and open the published item, which gives the signed PDF of the issue. For anything before 1936, use the historical Gazeta collection instead.

findLaw.task: Work out what changed and when it takes effect
findLaw.steps: Open 'análisis' on the consolidated norm: it lists what modified it, article by article, with dates and links to each amending item. The default in Article 2 of the Civil Code is twenty days after complete publication, so check the amending norm's final provisions before assuming a date.

Search the judiciary's case-law database by court, chamber, date or ECLI. For constitutional decisions, use the Constitutional Court's own search by decision number and year, or by the constitutional article at issue — a norm struck down there is also recorded against the norm in the BOE consolidated text.

Identify the community, open its gazette from the BOE's index of other official gazettes, and search there; autonomic statutes are also reproduced in the BOE and appear in the state consolidated collection. Municipal ordinances are published in the provincial bulletin, reachable from the same index.

findLaw.task: Get a whole field of law at once
findLaw.steps: Take the código electrónico for the subject — civil, criminal, labour, tax, administrative procedure — and download it as a single PDF or ePub with all its norms consolidated to the stated date. It is the fastest way into an unfamiliar area and it says on its cover when it was last updated.

findLaw.task: Find out why a regulation says what it says
findLaw.steps: Look for the Council of State opinion on the draft, which is usually the fullest published analysis of a regulation, and for a statute follow the bill through the Congress, where the Boletín Oficial de las Cortes Generales carries each successive text with the amendments tabled.
findLaw.source: Dictámenes del Consejo de Estado / Congreso

subnational: Spain is not a federation but is more decentralised than several that are. Seventeen autonomous communities and two autonomous cities legislate within the competences their statutes of autonomy take up from the Constitution, with their own parliaments and their own gazettes: the Diari Oficial de la Generalitat de Catalunya, the Boletín Oficial de la Junta de Andalucía, the Boletín Oficial del País Vasco and the rest. An autonomic statute is promulgated in that gazette and is also reproduced in the BOE, so it can be found in the state collection too. In Catalonia, the Balearic Islands, the Valencian Community, Galicia, the Basque Country and Navarre, publication is in the co-official language as well as Spanish, and both versions are official. Below the communities, provinces and some fifty thousand local entities publish ordinances and by-laws in the provincial bulletins — the boletines provinciales — which are the last place a rule that binds you can be hiding, and are not in the state consolidated collection at all. Navarre and the Basque provinces additionally hold historic fiscal powers, so their tax law diverges from the state's by right rather than by delegation.
caveats: The BOE's consolidated texts carry a notice on every page saying they are informative and have no legal value — the authentic text is the item published in the gazette, and the electronic BOE has been the official edition since 2009. Consolidation also began at a point in time: for older norms the consolidated version may not go back to the original wording, and for nineteenth-century texts the Gazeta scan is the only original. A norm can be in force and unconstitutional at once until the Constitutional Court says otherwise, and the Court's rulings sometimes preserve effects already produced. Case law is anonymised and, below the Supreme Court, published selectively. Autonomic and provincial law is published elsewhere and is not in the state consolidated collection, so a search that stops at the BOE will miss the rule that actually applies in a given place; in the co-official-language communities there are two official versions of the same text. Translations are scarce and unofficial — the Constitution is translated, ordinary statutes generally are not. The commercial services hold much that the free ones do not, and their texts are editorial.
